A  Anyone who has counted the rings on a tree stump knows that, in many species, each year of growth adds a new layer of wood. What is less widely appreciated is that the width of these rings varies from year to year according to conditions such as rainfall and temperature. In a dry year, a tree in a semi-arid region may add only a thin ring; in a wet year, the ring will be broad. Because trees of the same species in a region respond to the same weather, they record a shared pattern of wide and narrow rings, a kind of natural barcode that can be read by those who know how.

B  The scientific use of this barcode, known as dendrochronology, was pioneered in the early twentieth century by Andrew Ellicott Douglass, an American astronomer. Douglass was not originally interested in archaeology at all. He hoped that tree rings might reveal past cycles of solar activity, which he believed influenced the Earth's climate. His attempts to prove this connection were never widely accepted, but in the process he developed the essential technique of the discipline, called crossdating. By matching the pattern of rings in a living tree with that in older timber whose outer rings overlapped with it, he could extend a continuous record further and further back in time.

C  Archaeologists in the American Southwest quickly saw the potential of Douglass's work. The region's ancient Pueblo settlements contained thousands of wooden roof beams, but nobody knew exactly when they had been built. Douglass assembled two sequences: one extending back from the present, and a separate 'floating' sequence from ancient beams that could not be linked to any calendar year. For years a gap separated them. In 1929, a charred beam excavated at a site in Arizona finally contained the missing rings, and almost at once dozens of ruins could be assigned precise dates. The laboratory that Douglass later founded at the University of Arizona remains an important centre for tree-ring research.

D  Since then, long chronologies have been constructed in many parts of the world. In the mountains of the western United States, bristlecone pines, some of which have lived for more than four thousand years, have allowed researchers to build a sequence spanning around nine thousand years. In central Europe, oak and pine preserved in river gravels and bogs have produced an even longer record, covering more than twelve thousand years. These chronologies have had an important effect beyond archaeology: they revealed that dates obtained by radiocarbon analysis could be wrong by several centuries, and they now provide the standard against which radiocarbon dates are calibrated.

E  Tree rings can reveal more than dates. Because the width and density of each ring reflect growing conditions, long chronologies offer a detailed record of past climate, allowing researchers to identify historic droughts and cold periods with annual precision. Scars left by fires show how often forests burned before modern fire suppression. Comparing ring patterns with regional chronologies can even indicate where timber came from: analysis of a Viking ship excavated in Denmark showed that it had been built from oak grown near Dublin, in Ireland, demonstrating the reach of Viking shipbuilding networks.

F  The method nevertheless has limitations. Crossdating usually requires a sample containing many rings, ideally fifty or more, so small fragments of wood often cannot be dated. Many tropical trees, growing in climates without a distinct cold or dry season, do not form clear annual rings at all. And a tree-ring date indicates when the outermost surviving ring was formed, not necessarily when the timber was used. If the outer layers were trimmed away, or if old wood was recycled in a later building, archaeologists must interpret the evidence with caution.

A  On a dark night in certain coastal waters, a swimmer or a passing boat can leave a trail of glittering blue light in the sea. The display is produced by vast numbers of single-celled organisms called dinoflagellates, each of which emits a brief flash when disturbed. This phenomenon, the production of light by living organisms, is known as bioluminescence. While it appears magical to human observers, it is the result of a chemical reaction: a light-emitting compound, generally called a luciferin, combines with oxygen, and the reaction is accelerated by an enzyme known as a luciferase. Unlike a conventional light bulb, the process generates very little heat.

B  Bioluminescence is rare on land, where it is found mainly in fireflies, some other insects and fungi, and a few further groups. In the ocean, by contrast, it is extraordinarily common. A survey of animals observed by remotely operated vehicles off the coast of California found that roughly three-quarters of the creatures living in the water column, from the surface to a depth of about four kilometres, were capable of producing light. Since the open ocean is the largest habitat on the planet, bioluminescence may be one of the most widespread forms of communication on Earth. Most marine light is blue or green, the colours that travel furthest through seawater.

C  The ability to produce light has evolved independently many times, which suggests that it offers substantial advantages. One of the most ingenious uses is camouflage. In the dimly lit middle depths of the ocean, an animal swimming above a predator appears as a dark silhouette against the faint light from the surface. Many fish, squid and shrimp have rows of light organs on their undersides that emit light matching the brightness of the water above them, effectively erasing their shadow. This strategy, known as counter-illumination, can be adjusted continuously as the animal moves up and down.

D  Other species use light to attack rather than hide. The best-known example is the anglerfish, which dangles a glowing lure in front of its mouth to attract prey. Some deep-sea dragonfish have gone further, producing red light from organs beneath their eyes. Because most deep-sea animals cannot see red wavelengths, the dragonfish can illuminate its prey without being noticed, much like a person using an invisible searchlight. Light can also serve as a defence. The flashes of dinoflagellates, according to one widely discussed hypothesis, act as a 'burglar alarm': by lighting up the small animals that feed on them, they make those grazers more visible to larger predators.

E  On land, the most familiar function of bioluminescence is communication. Male fireflies of many species fly at dusk emitting a characteristic pattern of flashes, and females of the same species respond with flashes of their own. Each species has its own code, which helps individuals to find suitable mates. The system can, however, be exploited: females of certain predatory firefly species imitate the signals of other species, attracting males which they then eat.

F  Human understanding of bioluminescence has had unexpected scientific benefits. In the 1960s, the Japanese chemist Osamu Shimomura isolated a light-producing protein from a jellyfish found off the west coast of North America, and in the process discovered a second protein that glows green under ultraviolet light. Decades later, other researchers showed that the gene for this green fluorescent protein could be inserted into other organisms, allowing scientists to observe processes inside living cells that had previously been invisible. In 2008, Shimomura shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry with two American scientists for this work, and fluorescent proteins are now among the most widely used tools in biology.

The Frozen Water Trade

A  Today ice is so cheap and easy to produce that it is difficult to imagine it was once a valuable product shipped around the world. Yet for most of the nineteenth century, before machines could make ice reliably, a large international trade carried frozen water from the lakes and rivers of cold regions to hot cities thousands of kilometres away. The story of this trade begins with one determined businessman from Boston, in the north-east of the United States, whose name was Frederic Tudor.

B  In 1806, Tudor, then in his early twenties, loaded a ship with ice cut from a pond near his family's estate and sent it to the Caribbean island of Martinique. Many people in Boston thought the idea was ridiculous, and the first voyage was a financial failure. Although much of the ice survived the journey, there was nowhere on the island to store it, and local people had little idea what to do with it. Tudor lost a great deal of money, and in the years that followed he even spent time in prison because of his debts.

C  Tudor, however, refused to give up. He realised that success depended on two things: keeping the ice cold for longer and creating demand for it. He experimented with different ways of insulating ice, and found that sawdust, a waste product of the timber industry that was almost free, worked extremely well. He built well-insulated ice houses in the ports he supplied, and he encouraged bar owners to serve cold drinks, sometimes giving them ice free of charge until customers became used to it. Once people had tasted chilled drinks, he believed, they would not want to go back.

D  The business was transformed in the 1820s by a new tool. One of Tudor's suppliers, Nathaniel Wyeth, invented a cutter pulled by horses, which marked a grid on the frozen surface of a lake so that the ice could be divided into blocks of the same size. Regular blocks could be packed closely together, which meant that less of the ice melted during storage and transport. Harvesting became faster and cheaper, and the ice trade grew rapidly as a result.

E  By the 1830s, ice from New England was being shipped as far as India. In 1833 a ship carrying ice from Boston arrived in Calcutta after a journey of around four months, and a large part of the cargo was still frozen. Ice was soon being sent to South America, the Caribbean and Asia, and within the United States it was used to keep fish, meat and dairy products fresh on their way to growing cities. The writer Henry David Thoreau described watching teams of workers cutting ice on Walden Pond, the lake where he lived for two years, and imagined it being drunk in distant countries.

F  The natural ice trade reached its peak in the late nineteenth century, when Norway also exported large quantities of ice to Britain. However, it soon faced serious problems. As cities grew, many lakes and rivers became polluted, and people began to worry about the quality of natural ice. At the same time, machines that could produce ice artificially became more efficient and less expensive. By the early twentieth century, the trade in natural ice had almost disappeared, although the habits it had created, such as enjoying cold drinks and storing food at low temperatures, have lasted to the present day.

This made a far more powerful battery possible, but the problem of the reactive lithium metal electrode remained unsolved.

D  The final piece of the puzzle was supplied by Akira Yoshino, a researcher at the Japanese chemical company Asahi Kasei. In 1985 he replaced the lithium metal with a carbon-based material, petroleum coke, which could also hold lithium ions between its layers. The resulting battery contained no pure lithium at all: during discharge, lithium ions simply travelled from one electrode to the other through a liquid electrolyte, while electrons flowed through the external circuit, and during charging the process was reversed. The design was lighter, safer and capable of being recharged hundreds of times. In 1991, the electronics company Sony began selling the first commercial lithium-ion batteries.

E  Over the following three decades, improvements in manufacturing and materials led to dramatic reductions in cost. By one estimate, the price of lithium-ion cells, adjusted for capacity, fell by around 97 per cent between 1991 and 2018. This decline has made electric vehicles competitive with petrol cars in many markets and has allowed electricity companies to store solar and wind power for use when the sun is not shining or the wind is not blowing. Without cheap batteries, the large-scale transition to renewable energy would be considerably harder.

F  The technology is not without drawbacks. Many lithium-ion batteries contain cobalt, a large share of which is mined in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where serious concerns have been raised about working conditions, including the use of child labour. Extracting lithium from the salt flats of South America requires large volumes of water in some of the driest places on Earth. Recycling remains limited, partly because batteries are difficult to dismantle. In response, manufacturers are increasingly turning to chemistries that avoid cobalt, such as lithium iron phosphate, and researchers are exploring alternatives based on more abundant elements such as sodium.
